clue.text: How the Romans regarded the troops on Hadrian's Wall was civically

definitions.text: How the Romans regarded the troops on Hadrian's Wall was civically

parts.words: How the Romans regarded the troops on Hadrian's Wall was civically
parts.note: to Rome the soldiers on the Wall were its protection facing the northern tribes; 'civically' points to the Tyneside town of that name near the Wall's eastern end

explanation.surface: A history question about how Rome saw the garrison guarding its northernmost frontier.
explanation.walkthrough: The troops were Rome's defence facing north; read as a place name, the same phrase is a town at the mouth of the Tyne, close to where Hadrian's Wall ends at Wallsend.
explanation.definitionFit: Both readings fit: a description of the garrison as protective cover to the north, and the Tyneside town's name.

clue.text: Advice, from the clothing department, to one about to swim the Channel

definitions.text: Advice, from the clothing department, to one about to swim the Channel

parts.words: Advice, from the clothing department, to one about to swim the Channel
parts.note: Channel swimmers grease their bodies against the cold, so the advice is to coat the body; the clothing department sells a waterproof coat of the same name

explanation.surface: A shop assistant offers tips to someone planning to swim from England to France.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as two words it is the instruction to grease the body before a long cold swim; read as one it is a waterproof garment.
explanation.definitionFit: A waterproof coat made of oil-treated cloth, the kind a clothing department sells to sailors and fishermen.

clue.text: "To see suffer so From vermin was a pity" (Browning)

definitions.text: "To see suffer so From vermin was a pity" (Browning)

parts.words: "To see suffer so From vermin was a pity" (Browning)
parts.note: a line from Browning's The Pied Piper of Hamelin with one word left out after 'see': the people of Hamelin plagued by rats

explanation.surface: A quotation from Browning's Pied Piper with a gap to fill.
explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in-the-blank: the full line is about the people of Hamelin suffering from the plague of rats.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word names the inhabitants of a town, here the citizens of Hamelin in the poem.

clue.text: Odds and ends proclaim a simple truth

definitions.meaning: miscellaneous small items, as in a list of expenses
split in two, the word states the obvious fact that the solar heat makes wet things dry out

explanation.surface: Someone sets out to announce an obvious fact about bits and pieces.
explanation.walkthrough: 'proclaim' links: the word, split after its third letter, proclaims a truism about the weather drying the washing.
explanation.definitionFit: Assorted miscellaneous items too small to list separately are called by this collective word.

clue.text: The slippery slope, but it's only artificial

definitions.text: The slippery slope, but it's only artificial

parts.words: The slippery slope, but it's only artificial
parts.note: not the moral decline of the phrase but a literal frozen track built for tobogganing

explanation.surface: A warning about moral decline, shrugged off as a mere figure of speech.
explanation.walkthrough: 'slippery slope' suggests the idiom for gradual ruin; here it is literal, a man-made frozen chute for sledges.
explanation.definitionFit: A man-made frozen track for toboggans or bobsleighs is a literal slippery slope.

clue.text: Four in the lid, or six

definitions.text: Four in the lid, or six

indicators.note: one Roman numeral is put in the middle of the given word

parts.note: taken as written
IV is four in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: A cryptic instruction counting things placed under a lid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'or six' is the twist: the numeral for six placed inside the same word gives identical letters. There is no separate definition; the word means furious or bruised.
explanation.definitionFit: Either numeral placed in the cover yields the word for furious or black-and-blue, so the whole clue is the recipe.

clue.text: Such a tree as produces old anecdotes

definitions.text: Such a tree as produces old anecdotes

parts.words: Such a tree as produces old anecdotes
parts.note: Longfellow's Village Blacksmith stands 'under a ... chestnut tree', and a chestnut is a stale old story

explanation.surface: A riddle about a tree that bears stories instead of fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: A chestnut is a worn-out joke, so the chestnut tree yields old anecdotes; Longfellow's line supplies the adjective describing it.
explanation.definitionFit: Longfellow's chestnut tree is described with this adjective meaning wide-branching, extending outward.

clue.text: Casca invited these employees to speak for him

definitions.text: Casca invited these employees to speak for him

parts.words: Casca invited these employees to speak for him
parts.note: in Julius Caesar Casca strikes first, crying 'Speak, ..., for me!'; workers are also called by this word

explanation.surface: A Roman conspirator calls on his staff to be his spokesmen.
explanation.walkthrough: Casca's line in Shakespeare's Julius Caesar as he stabs Caesar; 'employees' plays on the sense of farm or factory workers.
explanation.definitionFit: Manual workers are called by this word, as in farmhands, and Casca addressed his own when striking Caesar.

clue.text: Don't arm (anag.)

indicators.note: the abbreviation openly tells the solver to rearrange the letters of the words before it

explanation.surface: A bare instruction to rearrange two words.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue is all wordplay: the letters of DONTARM rearranged; the answer means biting or caustic, or a dye fixative.
explanation.definitionFit: The rearranged letters give the word for sharply sarcastic, or a substance fixing dye, with no separate definition.

clue.text: A welcome family affair

parts.note: pocket money paid by parents to their children is a welcome arrangement kept within the family

explanation.surface: A cheerful gathering of relatives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'family affair' suggests a reunion, but it is the regular sum parents give children.
explanation.definitionFit: Pocket money handed out by parents is a regular sum children welcome, arranged within the family.

clue.text: The sign of the Roman girl

definitions.meaning: a constellation of the zodiac, the Virgin
the Latin word for a maiden

explanation.surface: An omen connected with a young woman of ancient Rome.
explanation.definitionFit: The zodiac sign of the Virgin keeps the Latin word for a maiden as its name.

clue.text: Graces at fisticuffs

definitions.meaning: noblemen of the top rank are addressed as 'Your Grace'
slang for fists, as in 'put up your ...'

explanation.surface: Elegant ladies come to blows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Graces' looks like charm or the three Graces; it is the form of address for senior peers.
explanation.definitionFit: Peers of the highest rank are styled Your Grace, and the same word is old slang for fists.

clue.text: Suitable script for a Puritan soldier

definitions.text: Suitable script for a Puritan soldier

parts.words: Suitable script for a Puritan soldier
parts.note: Cromwell's Puritan troops were Roundheads, so their fitting script is a rounded style of handwriting

explanation.surface: Handwriting advice for one of Cromwell's men.
explanation.walkthrough: Parliament's soldiers in the English Civil War were nicknamed Roundheads; a handwriting style shares the 'round' element.
explanation.definitionFit: A clear, rounded style of handwriting, echoing the Roundhead nickname of Cromwell's Puritan army.

clue.text: E.N. is implored to get married

definitions.text: E.N. is implored to get married

parts.note: taken as the initials as written
begged with the emphatic plea 'do wed!'

explanation.surface: Someone with the initials E.N. is begged to tie the knot.
explanation.walkthrough: The plea 'do wed' after the initials EN builds the word; the marriage service says 'with all my worldly goods I thee endow', so the whole clue hints at the meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: Being urged to marry and so receive the vow's worldly goods leaves one gifted or provided for.

clue.text: "And birds sit brooding in the snow And ---'s nose looks red and raw "(L.L.L.)

definitions.text: "And birds sit brooding in the snow And ---'s nose looks red and raw "(L.L.L.)

parts.words: "And birds sit brooding in the snow And ---'s nose looks red and raw "(L.L.L.)
parts.note: the winter song closing Love's Labour's Lost names a girl whose nose is red with cold

explanation.surface: A quotation from Shakespeare's Love's Labour's Lost with a name to fill.
explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in-the-blank from the song 'When icicles hang by the wall' at the end of Love's Labour's Lost.
explanation.definitionFit: The girl's name in Shakespeare's winter song, a variant of Marion, fills the gap.

clue.text: The old legal eminence

parts.note: the hill in Athens where the ancient council and court sat, and the court itself

explanation.surface: A grand old judge of high standing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'eminence' looks like a distinguished person; it means a hill, the rock of Ares in Athens that gave the ancient court its name.
explanation.definitionFit: The Athenian hill of Ares, seat of the city's highest ancient court, is literally an eminence used for law.

clue.text: What Cleopatra didn't say to the snake 'is underfoot

definitions.note: the clue reads 'what ... is underfoot', so it names the stuff walked on, a noun

parts.note: an asp is the small venomous snake Cleopatra used to kill herself
she let the snake bite rather than telling it to stop

explanation.surface: A joke about Cleopatra's last moment, ending on what lies beneath our feet.
explanation.walkthrough: Cleopatra put the asp to her breast instead of ordering it to stop: 'Asp, halt!'
explanation.definitionFit: The tarry surfacing of roads and pavements is what lies beneath walkers' feet.

clue.text: Where did this ship founder? O, on Capri

indicators.note: a ship that founders is wrecked, so these words break up and settle in a new order

explanation.surface: A question about where a vessel sank, answered: off Capri.
explanation.walkthrough: 'founder' reads as sinking near Capri, but signals rearranging the letters of O ON CAPRI.
explanation.definitionFit: An old word for a pirate or a pirate vessel, so a fitting ship to sink off Capri.

clue.text: The right member of the Kipling company to form a branch establishment

definitions.text: The right member of the Kipling company to form a branch establishment

parts.words: The right member of the Kipling company to form a branch establishment
parts.note: Kipling's school stories are titled after this boy '& Co.'; a stalk is a branch, so he is the one suited to a branch

explanation.surface: Choosing which partner in a firm should open a new branch office.
explanation.walkthrough: Kipling's schoolboy hero gives his name to the book Stalky & Co.; 'branch' plays on the stalk in his nickname.
explanation.definitionFit: The ringleader of Kipling's 'Co.' has a nickname built on a plant stalk, hence suited to a branch.

clue.text: Or ox one might call it

definitions.text: Or ox one might call it

indicators.note: calling a word means saying it out loud, so it is the spoken form that counts

parts.note: the two words spoken quickly

explanation.surface: A shrug about what to name a beast, perhaps just an ox.
explanation.walkthrough: Say 'or ox' and you get the name of the extinct European wild ox, so the clue both sounds and defines it.
explanation.definitionFit: The extinct wild ox of European forests, ancestor of domestic cattle, is indeed an ox.

clue.text: Game lie at such a distance

indicators.note: a bare signal: the words are read as set at work on themselves, put into a different order

parts.note: the letters of these two words rearranged

explanation.surface: A sporting fib told from far away.
explanation.walkthrough: Old Times clues barely signalled anagrams: 'at' is the only candidate, rearranging GAMELIE; the solver must spot the matching letter count.
explanation.definitionFit: A distance travelled or covered, counted in miles, is measured by this word.

clue.text: A foolish fellow, but with mental sharpness turns over the cash

indicators.note: turning something over flips it end to end, so the word for cash is read backwards

parts.note: tin is old slang for money
wit is quickness of mind

explanation.surface: A dim man who is nonetheless clever with the takings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turns over the cash' sounds like handling takings; it reverses TIN, slang for money.
explanation.definitionFit: A silly, brainless person, an informal synonym for a fool.

clue.text: Shop in America

parts.note: Americans call a retail outlet by this word rather than 'shop'

explanation.surface: Going shopping in the United States.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shop' looks like a verb; it is the noun, translated into the American term.
explanation.definitionFit: American usage for a retail shop, as in department or grocery outlet.

clue.text: I march on a musical instrument

indicators.note: a musical arrangement reorders material, so these words are set out anew

parts.note: the letters of these words rearranged

explanation.surface: A marcher steps out to a tune played on some instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'musical instrument' reads as one phrase; 'musical' is the rearranging signal on IMARCHONA, leaving 'instrument' alone as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The mouth organ, a small reed instrument played by blowing and drawing breath.

clue.text: Book but no book-ends

indicators.note: book-ends stand at each side of a row of volumes, so the letters go on either side of the book

parts.note: no is nought, the letter O, here standing at both ends
VOL is the abbreviation for volume

explanation.surface: A shelf holding a book but lacking the supports at either end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no book-ends' reads as lacking supports; it means noughts as the ends, an O each side of VOL. The answer, a convex quarter-round moulding, has no separate definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A rounded convex moulding in classical architecture, built here from a volume flanked by two noughts.

clue.text: Sanctimonious, but in the pit all the same

definitions.text: Sanctimonious, but in the pit all the same

parts.note: pi is old slang for pious or sanctimonious
taken as written

explanation.surface: A pious person who nonetheless ends up in hell, or the cheap theatre seats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'all the same' says the pious PI still ends with PIT; there is no separate definition of the small songbird.
explanation.definitionFit: A small brown songbird like a lark, its name made from the slang for pious followed by a hole.

clue.text: Where one isn't told what is under the post-office

definitions.note: a place name answers the question 'where?'

parts.note: PO is the standard abbreviation for post office
if the letter for one lies under the post office, then the post office sits on it, so the relation is spelt as the word ON
A is one, as in 'a pound' for one pound

explanation.surface: Something buried beneath a post office, and nobody will say what it is.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue says one (A) is under the post office (PO), which is the same as PO on A; 'isn't told what' just hides the fact that the thing underneath is only a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A city in western India, a British Army station in the Raj, now spelt Pune, so it names a place.

clue.text: A character from Measure for Measure

definitions.text: A character from Measure for Measure

parts.words: A character from Measure for Measure
parts.note: the 'fantastic' gentleman of Vienna in Shakespeare's play who slanders the disguised Duke

explanation.surface: A plain request for someone from one of Shakespeare's problem plays.
explanation.walkthrough: The '8' is a printing stray; the clue simply asks for a character in the play.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's loose-tongued Viennese gentleman, friend to Claudio, appears in that play.

clue.text: Not quite the same as a bad performer

definitions.text: Not quite the same as a bad performer

parts.words: Not quite the same as a bad performer
parts.note: split in two the word would be one who does things badly, but as one word it means a criminal

explanation.surface: A distinction drawn between a villain and a poor actor.
explanation.walkthrough: Read in two parts it could describe someone who acts badly; the clue notes the real word means something else.
explanation.definitionFit: An offender or sinner, one who commits a crime, rather than merely someone who performs poorly.

clue.text: The man who won at Bisley ?

definitions.text: The man who won at Bisley ?

parts.words: The man who won at Bisley ?
parts.note: Bisley in Surrey is the home of British target rifle competitions, so its champion is the star of the firing

explanation.surface: Asking who took the prize at a rifle meeting.
explanation.walkthrough: Bisley, in Surrey, hosts Britain's main rifle-shooting championships; its winner is the outstanding marksman.
explanation.definitionFit: A meteor seen streaking across the night sky, punningly the best performer at a rifle contest.
